text: The AI Act defines an "AI system" as any system capable of performing tasks that are not limited to the capabilities of a human. This definition applies to all systems listed in Annex III, including those used for migration, asylum, border control, law enforcement, and profiling. These systems are considered high-risk if they are intended to be used by public authorities or Union institutions in specific areas such as polygraph use, criminal risk assessment, evidence evaluation, or criminal profiling. The Act does not provide a specific list of examples for what constitutes an AI system beyond this general definition and the high-risk categories.

A "serious incident" is defined as an incident or malfunctioning of an AI system that directly or indirectly leads to any of the following: the death of a person, serious harm to a person's health, a serious and irreversible disruption of the management or operation of critical infrastructure, the infringement of obligations under Union law intended to protect fundamental rights, or serious harm to property or the environment [1]. For high-risk AI systems, this definition specifically includes cases where the incident infringes obligations under Union law intended to protect fundamental rights [1].

A general-purpose AI model is defined as an AI model that displays significant generality and is capable of competently performing a wide range of distinct tasks regardless of how it is placed on the market [1]. It is excluded from this definition if it is used for research, development, or prototyping activities before being placed on the market [1]. A general-purpose AI system is considered to be based on such a model and has the capability to serve a variety of purposes [4].

The AI Act does not apply to you because you are a natural person using the AI system in a purely personal, non-professional activity [1]. Consequently, the transparency obligations for providers and deployers do not apply to you [2].

The AI Act does not apply to research, testing, or development activities regarding AI systems prior to their placement on the market or putting them into service [1]. Testing in real-world conditions is explicitly excluded from this exclusion [1]. However, providers may conduct testing of high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions before placing them on the market [3]. Additionally, testing must be performed at any time throughout the development process, including prior to market placement [2].

Training, validation, and testing data sets must be subject to data governance and management practices appropriate for the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system [1]. These practices must concern in particular the relevant design choices, data collection processes, and relevant data-preparation processing operations [1]. They must also include an assessment of the availability, quantity, and suitability of the data sets needed [1]. Additionally, the practices must examine possible biases that could affect health and safety, have a negative impact on fundamental rights, or lead to discrimination [1]. Finally, appropriate measures must be taken to detect, prevent, and mitigate possible biases identified according to point (f) [1].

Yes, high-risk AI systems must keep logs automatically generated by them to the extent they are under their control. Article 12(1) requires these systems to automatically record events over their lifetime [3]. Specifically, providers must keep logs for a period of at least six months unless otherwise provided by Union or national law [1]. Additionally, deployers must maintain these logs for the same period [2]. These systems must also enable the recording of events relevant to identifying risks, facilitating post-market monitoring, and monitoring system operations [3].
The provided passages do not answer this question.

Yes, a provider established outside the EU must appoint an authorised representative established in the Union before placing a high-risk AI system on the market [3]. This requirement applies to high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III, with the exception of those referred to in point 2 of Annex III [2]. The authorised representative must be appointed by written mandate prior to the system's availability on the Union market [3].

Yes, providers of high-risk AI systems may exceptionally process special categories of personal data, including ethnicity, to ensure bias detection and correction, provided that the processing is strictly necessary and all applicable safeguards are met. These conditions include ensuring that bias detection cannot be effectively fulfilled by other data, deleting the data once bias is corrected or the retention period ends, and implementing technical limitations on re-use and state-of-the-art security measures [2][3][4][5].

The Digital Omnibus amendment added a prohibition against placing on the market, putting into service, or using AI systems that generate or manipulate realistic images of an identifiable natural person's intimate parts without their freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, and explicit consent [1]. This prohibition also applies to images of individuals engaged in sexually explicit activities [1]. Additionally, the amendment clarifies that an AI system must not manipulate material in a way that does not increase the exposure of depicted intimate parts or alter the nature of sexually explicit activities [2].

No, predicting whether someone will commit a crime based solely on the profiling of a natural person is prohibited under the AI Act. This prohibition applies to the placing on the market, putting into service, or use of such AI systems [1]. The Act explicitly forbids using AI systems to assess or predict the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence based on profiling [1]. This ban does not apply to AI systems used to support the human assessment of involvement in criminal activity, which must already be based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to the activity [1].

The Act prohibits the use of biometric categorisation systems that categorise individuals based on their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life, or sexual orientation [1]. This prohibition applies to the placing on the market, putting into service, or use of such systems [1]. The ban specifically covers systems that categorise individuals based on these attributes using biometric data [1].

Yes, an AI tool that screens and filters job applications is considered a high-risk AI system because it falls under the category of systems intended for the recruitment or selection of natural persons [1]. This classification applies to AI systems used to place targeted job advertisements, analyse and filter job applications, and evaluate candidates [1]. Consequently, such tools must be designed and developed with appropriate human-machine interface tools to be effectively overseen by natural persons [2].

An AI system intended to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons is considered high-risk [1]. However, an AI system used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud is excluded from this high-risk classification [1].

AI systems that are solely used for non-safety related aspects such as convenience or performance optimisation do not qualify as safety components. However, AI systems whose failure or malfunctioning would endanger health and safety shall qualify as safety components [2]. This distinction applies regardless of whether the system is placed on the market or put into service independently [4].

Yes, AI systems intended to be used in the supply of water, gas, heating, or electricity are classified as high-risk AI systems pursuant to Article 6(2) [1]. These systems are considered safety components because their failure or malfunction would endanger health and safety [3]. Consequently, they must be as resilient as possible regarding errors and faults [4].

The report on a serious disruption of critical infrastructure caused by a high-risk AI system must be provided immediately after the provider establishes a causal link or the reasonable likelihood of such a link, and in any event, not later than 15 days after the provider becomes aware of the incident [5].

Yes, providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video, or text content must ensure their outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated [1]. Providers of AI systems that have been placed on the market before 2 August 2026 must take necessary steps to comply with this obligation by 2 December 2026 [2]. Additionally, deployers of AI systems generating deep fakes or text published for the public must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated [3]. The European Commission is also encouraged to facilitate the drawing up of codes of practice to ensure effective implementation of these transparency obligations [4].

People must be informed that they are interacting with an AI system at the time of the first interaction or exposure [2]. This transparency obligation applies to AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons unless the interaction is obvious [1]. Additionally, deployers must disclose that AI-generated content is artificially created when publishing text on matters of public interest [3].

Generative AI systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 must comply with the output marking obligation by 2 December 2026. This requirement applies to providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, that have been placed on the market before that date [2]. The obligation is based on Article 50(2) of the Regulation [2].

A general-purpose AI model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training measured in floating point operations exceeds 10^25 [1]. The Commission may adopt delegated acts to amend these thresholds based on evolving technological developments [1].

Yes, providers of general-purpose AI models must draw up and keep up-to-date technical documentation [1]. This documentation must contain specific information such as the model's tasks, architecture, and parameters [3]. Additionally, it must include a detailed description of the model's elements and the development process [4]. If the energy consumption of the model is unknown, it may be based on information about computational resources used [2].

Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk must perform model evaluation using standardized protocols, including adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks [1]. They are also required to assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at the Union level, including their sources [1]. Additionally, these providers must keep track of, document, and report relevant information about serious incidents and possible corrective measures to the AI Office and national competent authorities without undue delay [1]. Finally, they must ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure [1].

Providers of general-purpose AI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must take the necessary steps to comply with the Act by 2 August 2027 [1]. This timeline applies to all general-purpose AI models already placed on the market prior to that date [1].

The maximum administrative fine for non-compliance with prohibited AI practices is up to EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of the undertaking's total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [1]. This applies to undertakings, whereas Union institutions face a maximum fine of up to EUR 1,500,000 [2]. Additionally, non-compliance with other requirements under the Regulation results in fines of up to EUR 750,000 [5].

A company can be fined up to EUR 7,500,000 or 1% of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, if it supplies incorrect, incomplete, or misleading information to a national competent authority [1]. This fine applies when the infringement becomes known to the national competent authorities [5].

Authorities must consider various factors when deciding the amount of an administrative fine, including the specific circumstances of the case, financial benefits gained or losses avoided from the infringement [1], the degree of cooperation with national competent authorities [2], whether fines have already been applied to the same operator for the same infringement [3], the size, annual turnover, and market share of the operator [4], and whether fines have been applied by other authorities for infringements of other Union or national law [5].

The Commission may impose fines not exceeding 3% of the provider's annual worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year, or EUR 15,000,000, whichever is higher. This applies when the provider intentionally or negligently infringes relevant provisions, fails to comply with requests for information, or fails to make available access to the model [1]. The Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review these fine decisions [2].

You can complain about a breach of the AI Act by lodging a reasoned complaint with a downstream provider of a general-purpose AI model, as outlined in Article 89 [2]. This complaint must include details about the relevant facts, the specific provisions of the Regulation involved, and the reason why the provider is considered to have infringed the law [2]. If you are a downstream provider, you may also contact the provider directly to report the alleged infringement [2].

Providers and deployers must keep logs of high-risk AI systems for a period of at least six months, unless applicable Union or national law provides a different duration [1][2]. This requirement applies to logs automatically generated by the system to the extent they are under their control [1][2].

The Act does not list specific chatbots or AI models that have been designated as having systemic risk. It only provides criteria for determining whether a general-purpose AI model has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those set out in Article 51(1), point (a) [1][2][4]. The Commission may designate a model as presenting systemic risks ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel [5].

The AI Act does not specify any programming languages that high-risk AI systems must be written in. [1] and [2] only require that the EU declaration of conformity and certificates be drawn up in a language easily understood by relevant authorities, but this does not apply to the code itself. [3] and [4] mandate that information and documentation be provided in a language easily understood by competent authorities, yet they do not address the programming language of the AI system. [5] defines high-risk AI systems based on their classification rules rather than their implementation language. Therefore, the provided passages do not answer this question.

The AI Act does not specify the salary for the head of the AI Office. It only states that the Commission shall develop expertise through the AI Office and that it shall be allocated adequate resources to perform its duties [1]. The Act also mentions that the AI Office may appoint external experts and auditors to assist in monitoring compliance [2]. However, there is no information regarding specific compensation or salary figures for the office's leadership in the provided passages.
